title: The Gadget Blueprint
covers: how to use the distributive property and an area model to expand and factor expressions

intro.caption: Lesson 6-14 — the distributive property. Ozzie is building a flying drone. The blueprint needs the area of its metal body. Three gates and a boss inspection stand between Ozzie and lift-off.

balloons.t: The body is 4 units tall. One part stretches x units. The battery part is 3 units.
Area is 4(x + 3). So it's 4x + 3. That's classified.
So my battery part is only 3 square units? It's 4 tall!

pages.caption: Teo multiplied the 4 by the x part only. The 4 has to multiply every term inside the parentheses.

balloons.t: Two parts. Find the area of each part, then add.
My launcher's blueprint says 6x + 18. Ozzie needs it as a factor times a sum.
Find the greatest number that goes into both parts. Pull it outside.
Plug in a number. If the areas don't match, the drone doesn't fly.
I'm the inspector today. Three checks. You'll miss a term. You always do.
Not anymore. I multiply EVERY term now. Every. Single. One.
4x + 12. Every part got its share. Now get me down.

win.caption: The distributive property: a(b + c) = ab + ac. To expand, multiply the outside factor by every term inside. To factor, pull the greatest common factor outside. The area model shows both.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Expand
gates.prompt: The drone body is 4 tall and x + 3 long. Expand 4(x + 3).
hints: Conceptual: the rectangle has two parts. Both parts are 4 tall, so the 4 multiplies BOTH the x and the 3.
Procedural: multiply the outside number by the first term, then by the second term. Keep the sign between them.

steps: Practice: 3(a + 5). The 3 multiplies every term inside.

options.fb: You distributed to the first term only. The 3 part is 4 tall too: 4 × 3 = 12.
You multiplied only the 3. The x part is also 4 tall, so it is 4x.

items.q: A wing panel is 5(2y − 1). Expand it.

options.fb: You distributed to the first term only. The 5 multiplies the 1 too: 5 × 1 = 5.
Keep the sign. It is 5 × (−1), so the term is −5.

gates.pass: 4x + 12 on the body and 10y − 5 on the wing. The battery part finally gets its 12 square units.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Pull It Out
gates.badge: Factor Finder — Factor Out the GCF
gates.prompt: Farah's launcher blueprint says 6x + 18. Write it as a factor times a sum.
hints: Conceptual: factoring undoes expanding. Find the greatest common factor of the terms and put it outside.
Procedural: find the GCF of 6 and 18. Divide each term by it and write what is left inside the parentheses.

steps: Practice: 7x + 14. The GCF of 7 and 14 is 7.

items.q: Factor 6x + 18 using the greatest common factor.

options.fb: You divided only the first term by 6. Expand it: 6 × 18 = 108, not 18.
That is equal, but 3 is not the GREATEST common factor. 2x + 6 still shares a 2.
That is 6x × 4 = 24x. The 18 has no x, so x cannot come outside.

items.label: 8m + 20 = ? × (2m + 5). The factor outside is
items.aria: the greatest common factor pulled out of 8m plus 20

fb.msg: 8(2m + 5) = 16m + 40. Too big. Which number times 2m gives 8m?
2(2m + 5) = 4m + 10. Too small. Which number times 5 gives 20?
20 × 5 = 100, not 20. Find a number that goes into both 8 and 20.

items.fbDefault: What times 2m gives 8m, and what times 5 gives 20?

gates.pass: 6(x + 3) and 4(2m + 5). Farah's launcher stops smoking. Mostly.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Test the Model
gates.prompt: Let x = 5. Use the area model to test 4(x + 3) against Teo's 4x + 3.
hints: Conceptual: equivalent expressions have the same value for every x. One number that gives different values proves they are not equivalent.
Procedural: find the area of each part of the rectangle (4 × 5 and 4 × 3) and add. Then put 5 in for x in Teo's expression.

steps: Both are 20. The model and the expanded form match.

items.label: Area of the whole body, 4(x + 3), when x = 5:
items.aria: area of the drone body when x is 5

fb.msg: 23 is 4 × 5 + 3. That's Teo's expression. The 3 part is 4 tall: 4 × 3 = 12.
20 is only the x part (4 × 5). Add the battery part, 4 × 3.

items.fbDefault: Find 4 × 5 and 4 × 3, then add the two areas.

items.q: At x = 5 the model gives 32, but Teo's 4x + 3 gives 23. What does that show?

options.t: They are equivalent. A small difference is okay.
options.fb: Equivalent means the same value for every x. 32 and 23 are different, so they are not equivalent.

options.t: The model is wrong. The battery part has area 3.
options.fb: The battery part is 4 tall and 3 long, so its area is 4 × 3 = 12.

gates.pass: 32 square units, both ways: 4 × 8 and 20 + 12. Teo's 23 is retired.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Vale's Inspection
gates.prompt: Three inspection checks. Expand, factor, and evaluate — and miss no terms.
hints: Conceptual: expanding multiplies the outside factor by every term. Factoring pulls the greatest common factor out of every term.
Procedural: after you expand or factor, check by expanding back or by putting in a number.

steps: Practice check: expand 5(p − 3). Multiply every term: 5 × p = 5p and 5 × 3 = 15.
Test with p = 4: 5 × 1 = 5, and 20 − 15 = 5. They match.

options.fb: You distributed to the first term only. 7 times k is 7k.

items.q: Check 2 · Factor 9w + 12 using the greatest common factor.

options.fb: You divided only the first term by 3. 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
9 does not go into 12. Expand it: 9 × 12 = 108, not 12.
That is 3w × 7 = 21w. The 12 has no w, so w cannot come outside.

items.label: Check 3 · 6(m − 2) when m = 10:
items.aria: value of six times m minus two when m is 10

fb.msg: 58 is 6 × 10 − 2. You distributed to the first term only. 6 × 2 = 12.

items.fbDefault: Find 10 − 2 first, or find 6 × 10 − 6 × 2. Both ways give the same value.

gates.pass: 14 + 7k, 3(3w + 4), and 48. Vale checks twice, finds nothing, and leaves without a word.

journal.heading: Lesson 6-14 — what the gadget blueprint taught us
rows: Multiply the outside factor by every term inside: 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12, and 5(2y − 1) = 10y − 5.
Find the greatest common factor and pull it outside: 6x + 18 = 6(x + 3).
A rectangle 4 tall and x + 3 long has two parts: 4x and 4 × 3 = 12. Together, 4x + 12.
4x + 3 forgets the second part. Test x = 5: 4(5 + 3) = 32, but 4 × 5 + 3 = 23. Not equivalent.
journal.quote: "Every term gets multiplied. No term left behind. Including me." — Chip

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 6-14 (The Distributive Property) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: expanding a(b + c) and a(b − c), factoring out the greatest common factor, the area model, and testing a value to check that two expressions are equivalent.
standards: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions
